title: Marguerite and the Orbit
premise: Tamsin Oyelaran, a xenolinguist whose mind was rewired by contact with an alien signal so thoroughly he no longer dreams in human languages, has spent three years hauling cargo through the contested orbit of colony world Meridian. When the colony's children begin sharing one identical dream — a dream Tamsin recognizes as the same signal that changed him — both the colonial fleet and the Earth fleet accuse each other of biowarfare, and only Tamsin can decode the dream's true message: a warning that the jump corridor itself is collapsing. To keep the two fleets from destroying each other before the last jump window closes, he must sustain a fabricated translation that buys time, even as his loyalty to the woman he loves, fleet officer Ada Sorensen, demands he tell the truth. In the end Tamsin confesses his lie publicly, the fleets nearly fire on each other, but the children's shared dream proves his real translation correct — the corridor collapses harmlessly, stranding both fleets together, and Tamsin, stripped of rank and language, begins learning to dream human again in Ada's arms.
about_author: Silas Winterbourne is the pen name of a former maritime radio operator who spent eleven years relaying messages between ships that never met, and who now writes about people separated by distances only language can cross. He lives on a cold coast, keeps a shortwave rig tuned to dead frequencies, and claims his best ideas arrive as dreams he can no longer translate.

chapters.title: Cargo of Quiet
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He hauls ore through Meridian's contested orbit, narrating his estrangement from human language — he dreams in the alien pattern now, wordless and geometric. A routine docking goes wrong when a colonial patrol scans his hold. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as competence; he is fluent in everything except himself.

chapters.title: The Children's Hour
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Fleet officer Ada Sorensen investigates reports that forty-three colony children woke at 3 a.m. reciting identical nonsense syllables. She interviews a girl who draws a spiral that matches classified signal intercepts. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into dread as Ada realizes the drawings predate any known transmission.

chapters.title: Two Fleets, One Sky
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. He witnesses a near-collision between colonial and Earth warships over docking rights, both fleets blaming the other for the children's condition. A colonial commodore quietly recruits Tamsin — the only certified xenolinguist in range — to analyze the dream-speech. Emotional beat: reluctant entanglement; the orbit he hauls through is becoming a fuse.

chapters.title: What He Dreamed Instead
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, flashback-laced. Under lab lights he admits the children's syllables are the same signal that rewired him three years ago aboard the survey ship Calliope. He hides that he already understands fragments of it. Emotional beat: shame and self-preservation; the lie begins as an omission.

chapters.title: Ada in the Airlock
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada boards Tamsin's freighter under pretext of inspection; old love resurfaces in the cramped galley. She warns him the Earth fleet believes the signal is a colonial bioweapon and is mobilizing. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by divided loyalty — she is his anchor and his adversary's officer.

chapters.title: The First False Translation
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Pressured by the commodore to deliver findings before the jump window, Tamsin fabricates a translation: the signal is a 'harmless navigation beacon.' It buys calm for seventy-two hours. Emotional beat: the vertigo of power — one sentence from his mouth holds two fleets still.

chapters.title: Spirals in the Classroom
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The dream spreads to two hundred children, and now adults. A teacher's suicide note reads in the dream-syllables. Ada begins her own off-the-books investigation and finds Tamsin's name in the Calliope's sealed logs. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into suspicion of the man she loves.

chapters.title: Jump Window Mathematics
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. The astrogator Voss shows him the corridor's jump window: nineteen days, then a year's delay that neither fleet's supplies can survive. Both fleets are quietly arming to seize the corridor. Emotional beat: claustrophobic countdown; every choice now has a deadline.

chapters.title: The Interrogation of Tamsin Oyelaran
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Earth intelligence detains and questions Tamsin; Ada is assigned to observe. He lies beautifully, and she catches the seam — he translates a child's recording too fluently for a man who claims confusion. Emotional beat: love as betrayal; she says nothing, and hates herself for it.

chapters.title: What the Dream Actually Says
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, alone. Working from memory, Tamsin cracks the true structure: the signal isn't a message from aliens but a distress echo — the jump corridor is destabilizing, and the 'dream' is a warning broadcast by something caught inside it. Emotional beat: terrible clarity; the truth is worse than either fleet's paranoia.

chapters.title: The Commodore's Bargain
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin reports the real finding; the commodore orders him to bury it — a corridor collapse justifies a first strike against Earth's fleet before the window closes. Tamsin complies, keeping the false translation alive. Emotional beat: complicity deepens; he is now the lie's custodian.

chapters.title: Ada's Evidence
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada assembles proof of the falsified translation and of Tamsin's Calliope history. She must choose: deliver him to Earth fleet intelligence, destroying him and possibly triggering war, or warn him. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth made literal — she loves a man who is the war's fuse.

chapters.title: Night Docking
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ada confronts Tamsin aboard his freighter. He confesses everything: the signal, the lie, the commodore's order. She gives him six hours to make it public before she does. Emotional beat: the novel's hinge — intimacy rebuilt on confessed ruin; they are allies again, and both marked.

chapters.title: The Broadcast That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. His attempt to broadcast the truth is jammed by the commodore; Tamsin is confined as 'signal-compromised.' The children, meanwhile, all begin dreaming the same final sequence — a countdown matching the jump window. Emotional beat: caged desperation; the truth now has a deadline of its own.

chapters.title: Children of the Corridor
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada smuggles a recording of the children's synchronized recitation to sympathetic officers on both fleets. A colonial gunnery officer and an Earth astrophysicist independently confirm the corridor-decay math. Emotional beat: fragile coalition forming in the margins; truth finding allies without its author.

chapters.title: Fifteen Minutes to Fire
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Both fleets converge on the corridor; the commodore orders Tamsin to broadcast the false translation as final justification for the strike. Instead, Tamsin hijacks the fleet-wide channel and confesses everything — the lie, the real translation, his own rewiring. Emotional beat: the lie dies loudly; the novel's climax of speech.

chapters.title: The Window Closes
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Fleets hold fire, paralyzed by Tamsin's confession, as the jump window's final minutes tick. The corridor shudders — and collapses exactly as the true translation predicted, harmlessly, sealing both fleets in the system together. Emotional beat: vindication laced with ruin; no one gets to leave.

chapters.title: Court of the Stranded
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. A joint tribunal convenes. Tamsin pleads guilty to the false translation and testifies against the commodore. The children, still dreaming, begin teaching adults the signal's language — it is becoming a bridge, not a weapon. Emotional beat: accountability without absolution; the price of the lie is paid in full.

chapters.title: What Ada Chose
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada faces charges for withholding evidence and chooses to testify for Tamsin at cost to her own career. She is demoted and reassigned planet-side; he is stripped of certification. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved — she chose him, and chose the truth, and pays for both.

chapters.title: Learning to Dream
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Planet-side, Tamsin works with the dreaming children, who patiently teach him their shared language — and, in doing so, return human words to him. He dreams his first human dream in three years: Ada's voice saying his name. Emotional beat: quiet restoration; the wound the signal made begins to close.

chapters.title: The Second Signal
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A year into the stranding, the children's dream shifts: a new sequence, pointing outward, toward whatever sent the warning. The stranded fleets, forced to cooperate to survive, vote to build a receiver together. Emotional beat: hope with teeth; enemies became neighbors, and now crew.

chapters.title: Marguerite and the Orbit
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV, final. Revealed: 'Marguerite' is the name the children gave the dreaming intelligence in the corridor — and the name of the freighter Tamsin has refitted for the joint expedition. He and Ada take her up into the orbit where it began, toward the second signal. Emotional beat: departure without escape; love, language, and duty finally pulling in the same direction.
